title: Social Security Faces 2032 Depletion as Congress Weighs Costly Fixes
excerpt: The trustees project the retirement fund will pay only 78% of benefits after late 2032, while a budget rule could hide the cost of borrowing to pay benefits in full.
body:
• The retirement fund (OASI) is projected to deplete in the fourth quarter of 2032, after which payroll taxes alone would pay 78% of scheduled benefits — an automatic cut of about 22%; the combined retirement and disability funds (OASDI) deplete in the third quarter of 2034 and would pay 83%.
  • The hidden cost: budget scoring treats paying full benefits from general revenue after depletion as costless, but Penn Wharton estimates that borrowing would reach almost 200% of GDP, or over 400% of taxable payroll, over 75 years.
  • Congress's modelled options range from heavy tax increases to heavy benefit cuts, including raising the payroll tax rate or the earnings cap — $184,500 in 2026 — raising the full retirement age, and adjusting the benefit formula; acting sooner widens the range and allows phase-ins.
  • What it means for an Indian immigrant worker: benefits are based on payroll taxes paid on covered earnings, not citizenship alone. If you have paid in for at least 10 years and Congress does not act, the same 22% OASI cut projected for 2032 would apply to your retirement benefit as to any other beneficiary's.

Social Security is expected to reach insolvency within a decade, triggering automatic benefit cuts under current law unless Congress acts. A new Penn Wharton Budget Model analysis reported by Fox Business warns that the easiest-looking fix — paying full benefits from general revenue — carries a hidden cost that federal budget rules make invisible.

Kent Smetters, faculty director of the Penn Wharton Budget Model, told Fox Business that budget rules assume benefits would be paid in full using general revenue transfers when the trust funds are depleted in about six or seven years. A separate rule for the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) scores that transfer as if it had no cost.

"What the law actually says is that when the trust fund depletes, benefits have to be reduced to a level that's consistent with just the monthly payroll taxes that come in."

— Kent Smetters, Faculty Director, Penn Wharton Budget Model

The trustees' timeline: 2032 and 2034

The Social Security Trustees' 2026 report summary gives two dates that are often confused. The Old-Age and Survivors Insurance fund, which pays retirement and survivor benefits, can pay 100% of scheduled benefits until the fourth quarter of 2032, one quarter earlier than projected last year, and would then pay 78%. The Disability Insurance fund is projected to pay full benefits through at least 2100. Combined on a hypothetical basis — the two funds cannot legally be combined without a change in law — OASDI would pay full benefits until the third quarter of 2034 and 83% after that.

AARP's summary notes payments go to more than 71 million people, funded mainly by payroll taxes. The trustees lowered their fertility assumption from 1.9 to 1.75 children per woman and lowered immigration assumptions, reducing future workers paying in. The 75-year deficit is now 4.42% of taxable payroll. CBO estimates differ: Fox Business reported CBO sees a 28% average reduction after 2032, about $2.7 trillion from 2032 to 2036, while Penn Wharton models 2033 and about 15%.

The hidden cost of the easy button

Smetters said the general-revenue approach is "the left hand paying the right hand," does not solve the funding problem, yet scores as zero even though borrowing would reach almost 200% of GDP within 75 years, or over 400% of taxable payroll. He warned bond markets are betting Congress will act, and that transfers could raise interest rates.

Options Congress is weighing

Penn Wharton publishes seven illustrative options ranging from heavy tax revenue increases to heavy benefit cuts, with a middle ground between them. The levers modelled in that debate are familiar: increase the payroll tax rate, lift or remove the cap on earnings subject to the tax, raise the full retirement age, or adjust the benefit formula for future beneficiaries. The trustees make the timing point explicitly in their summary: taking action sooner rather than later allows a broader range of solutions and more time to phase in changes so the public can prepare. Smetters pointed to the 1980s reforms under President Ronald Reagan and House Speaker Tip O'Neill as the last time both parties accepted shared political cost to fix the programme.

What to watch, and what to do now

No reform has been enacted, and benefits will not stop: after depletion, payroll taxes still pay most of the scheduled amount. Workers — including Indian immigrants who built eligibility through covered US employment — should check their earnings record and statement, and plan on the assumption a cut in the early 2030s is possible unless Congress legislates. A bipartisan proposal specifying tax, cap, retirement-age or formula changes, rather than a general-revenue transfer, would signal a real fix is moving.
